title: The other cheek (Matthew 5:38–42)
hookLine: no revenge: turn the cheek, give the cloak, go the second mile

cards: Somebody shoves you in line. Somebody posts something cruel about you. Somebody takes your parking space, then smirks.

Everything in you wants to even the score, and maybe a little more than even, just so they learn. The next lines are hard ones: turn the other cheek, go the extra mile. People who've never opened a Bible use them.
To hear them properly, start with the old rule he's quoting.

teach.h: AN EYE FOR AN EYE: A LIMIT.
teach.b: In the King James Bible: "Ye have heard that it hath been said, An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth." That's from the law of Moses.

It's often read as a limit on revenge rather than a command to take it: one eye for one eye, not a whole family for an eye. In Jewish tradition, the rabbis read it as fair compensation paid in court, not literal injury.

teach.h: TURN TO HIM THE OTHER ALSO.
teach.b: "But I say unto you, That ye resist not evil: but whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also." Then three pictures. If someone sues you for your coat, give him your cloak too.
And: "whosoever shall compel thee to go a mile, go with him twain." Compel had a specific use: scholars say it meant soldiers and officials pressing locals into service, like carrying gear.
It's the same Greek word Mark uses when the soldiers compel Simon of Cyrene to carry the cross. So picture a soldier of the occupying army ordering you to haul his pack. The order is one mile.

Jesus says: go two. Readings differ. Some, like the scholar Walter Wink, argue that a slap on the right cheek was a backhanded insult, and turning the other cheek was a nonviolent way of standing your ground with dignity.

Others read it more simply as refusing to retaliate at all. Churches differ, too: the peace churches say it rules out violence entirely; many other Christians say it governs personal revenge, not every use of force.
What these readings share is the direction: break the cycle.

how: The peace churches, such as Mennonites, Quakers and the Church of the Brethren, read this as a call to nonviolence; many other Christians apply it to personal insult and revenge, and practice it through forgiveness and generosity.

games.q: a Roman soldier orders you to carry his pack for a mile. you reach the milestone. what does Jesus say to do?
games.why: "whosoever shall compel thee to go a mile, go with him twain." do more than you're forced to, freely.

practice: Think of someone who asks more of you than you'd like: a demanding boss, a needy relative, a neighbor who always wants a favor.
Picture doing what they usually ask, and then a little more, freely, before they ask; not because you have to, because you choose to.
If it would put you in danger or let someone abuse you, that's not this, and if you pray, you can ask for a free heart.

wordCard.voice: Compel. The word for pressing someone into forced service, the same word used when soldiers made Simon carry the cross. No revenge: turn the cheek, give the cloak, go the second mile freely instead.

orig.note: Greek: shall compel, press into service. Matthew 5:41; Mark 15:21 uses it of Simon of Cyrene.

carryVoice: Your line: the second mile. The first was the order. Two hundred forty-six days, and counting.
